question.text: Per NISM Ch 2.2 on Traditional Investments, which statement correctly contrasts equity shares and debt instruments?

answer.text: Equity shareholders are senior claimants over debt holders in a liquidation waterfall.
Both equity and debt carry identical voting rights and identical payment priorities.
Debt instruments always pay higher returns than equity because they carry higher risk.

Equity shares represent ownership with residual claim on profits after contractual claims are satisfied and carry voting rights; debt instruments are contracts promising a stream of cashflows with contractual restrictions on the borrower and defined rights on default.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Chapter 2.2.1, equity shareholders are residual owners of the firm's profit after other contractual claims on the firm are satisfied and they have ultimate control over how the firm is operated. Per 2.2.2, debt is a promise to pay a stream of cashflows during the term of the contract and establishes the financial requirements and restrictions that the borrower must meet, plus the rights of the holder of the debt instruments if the borrower defaults. The Trap: Option A inverts the capital-structure waterfall (debt is senior). Option B is factually false — debt carries no voting rights and has higher payment priority than equity. Option C is wrong because debt does not always pay higher returns and is not described as higher-risk than equity in the source. Note: The key contrast is residual ownership and voting (equity) versus contractual cashflows with defined default rights (debt).
